items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a molecule formed by an enzyme-catalysed reaction"?
items.answer: Product
items.markingKey: Product: a molecule formed by an enzyme-catalysed reaction.

items.stem: Explain how an enzyme catalyses the breakdown of a substrate. Use the terms active site and enzyme–substrate complex.
items.answer: The substrate collides with and fits into the complementary active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex; the reaction occurs and products are released, leaving the enzyme unchanged.
items.markingKey: complementary fit [1]; ES complex formed [1]; products released, enzyme unchanged [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why protease cannot digest starch.
items.answer: The shape of the active site of protease is complementary to proteins, not starch; starch cannot fit, so no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
items.markingKey: active site shape specific [1]; starch does not fit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which substance is the substrate of pectinase?
items.answer: pectin
items.markingKey: Pectinase: pectin → soluble sugars.

items.stem: (a) Name the products when catalase acts on hydrogen peroxide. (b) Explain why catalase cannot act on sucrose.
items.answer: (a) water and oxygen (b) The active site of catalase is complementary to hydrogen peroxide only; sucrose does not fit.
items.markingKey: (a) water and oxygen [1] (b) active site shape specific / complementary to hydrogen peroxide [1]; sucrose cannot bind / no enzyme–substrate complex [1] [3]

items.stem: Catalase from potato released 30 cm³ of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide in 60 s. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute. Predict the volume of oxygen released in the same time if the enzyme concentration is doubled (substrate in excess), and explain.
items.answer: 30 cm³/min; about 60 cm³
items.markingKey: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 cm³/s [1]; × 60 = 30 cm³/min [1]; 60 cm³ [1]; twice as many active sites so more / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes per second [1] [4]

items.stem: Diego investigates the enzyme catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, in a laboratory in Lagos. (a) Explain why increasing the substrate concentration increases the rate only up to a point. (b) Explain why the enzyme is described as a catalyst.
items.answer: (a) More substrate means more collisions and ES complexes; eventually all active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting. (b) It speeds up the reaction and is not changed or used up by it.
items.markingKey: (a) more collisions / complexes [1]; active sites saturated [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Kwame investigates the enzyme lipase, which breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol, in a laboratory in Toronto. (a) Describe how the enzyme and substrate interact. Use the term enzyme–substrate complex. (b) Explain why increasing the substrate concentration increases the rate only up to a point.
items.answer: (a) Substrate fits into the complementary active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex; the substrate is broken down and products leave the active site. (b) More substrate means more collisions and ES complexes; eventually all active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting.
items.markingKey: (a) fit into active site [1]; ES complex [1]; products released [1] [3] (b) more collisions / complexes [1]; active sites saturated [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "substrate"?
options: A molecule formed by an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
The molecule on which an enzyme acts.
The temporary structure formed when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction.
items.answer: The molecule on which an enzyme acts.
items.markingKey: Substrate: the molecule on which an enzyme acts.

items.stem: Why does each enzyme act on only one type of substrate?
options: Substrates are all the same shape
Each enzyme is used up after one reaction
The shape of the active site is complementary to only that substrate
items.answer: The shape of the active site is complementary to only that substrate
items.markingKey: Enzyme specificity: the substrate must fit the active site.

items.stem: Explain why only small amounts of enzymes are needed in cells.
items.answer: Enzymes are not used up; each enzyme molecule can catalyse the reaction many times.
items.markingKey: not used up [1]; reused many times [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why enzymes are needed for reactions in cells even though the reactions would happen eventually without them.
items.answer: Without enzymes the reactions would be far too slow at body temperature to supply energy and materials for life.
items.markingKey: too slow [1]; at body temperature / for life processes [1] [2]

items.stem: Catalase from celery released 45 cm³ of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide in 60 s. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.
items.answer: 45 cm³/min

items.stem: Which enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide?
items.answer: catalase
items.markingKey: Catalase: hydrogen peroxide → water and oxygen.

items.stem: Catalase from yeast released 24 cm³ of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide in 120 s. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.
items.answer: 12 cm³/min

items.stem: Describe how enzymes work, using the lock and key idea, and explain why each enzyme is specific.
items.answer: Enzymes are proteins with an active site of specific shape; the substrate is complementary (lock and key) and fits, forming an ES complex; reaction happens and products released; enzyme reused; other substrates do not fit so enzyme is specific.
items.markingKey: protein / catalyst [1]; active site shape [1]; ES complex [1]; products released enzyme reused [1]; specificity explained [1] [5]

items.stem: Hana investigates the enzyme protease, which breaks down protein into amino acids, in a laboratory in Cairo. (a) Explain why increasing the substrate concentration increases the rate only up to a point. (b) Suggest a suitable control for this investigation. (c) Explain why the enzyme is described as a catalyst.
items.answer: (a) More substrate means more collisions and ES complexes; eventually all active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting. (b) Use boiled (denatured) enzyme instead of active enzyme, to show that the enzyme causes the reaction. (c) It speeds up the reaction and is not changed or used up by it.
items.markingKey: (a) more collisions / complexes [1]; active sites saturated [1] [2] (b) boiled enzyme [1]; shows the enzyme is responsible [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "kinetic energy"?
options: How quickly substrate is used or product is formed per unit time.
Contact between enzyme and substrate molecules, which is needed to form an enzyme–substrate complex.
The energy of moving molecules, which increases with temperature.
The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
items.answer: The energy of moving molecules, which increases with temperature.
items.markingKey: Kinetic energy: the energy of moving molecules, which increases with temperature.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases from 10 °C to 35 °C.
items.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so enzyme and substrate collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
items.markingKey: more kinetic energy [1]; more frequent collisions / ES complexes [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an enzyme that has been boiled does not work when it is cooled again.
items.answer: Boiling denatures the enzyme: the active site changes shape permanently, so the substrate can no longer fit even when cooled.
items.markingKey: denatured [1]; permanent change in active site shape [1] [2]

items.stem: Tomás mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. A drop of the mixture was added to iodine solution every 30 seconds, and the time until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 347, 191, 73, 71, 130, 223, 366; trial 2: 352, 181, 75, 76, 130, 226, 373; trial 3: 352, 196, 73, 72, 131, 232, 366. State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean time for starch to disappear on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and time for starch to disappear on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. A drop of the mixture was added to iodine solution every 30 seconds, and the time until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 681, 275, 63, 179, 441; trial 2: 694, 261, 88, 166, 460; trial 3: 714, 259, 63, 169, 476. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) Calculate the rate of reaction at the optimum temperature, using rate = 1000 ÷ time.
items.answer: (a) Test more often than every 30 s to time the end-point more precisely. (b) 15.9 s⁻¹ (arbitrary units)
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: test more often than every 30 s to time the end-point more precisely; leave the enzyme and starch at the temperature for 5 minutes before mixing (equilibrate); use a thermostatically controlled water bath; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) shortest mean time = 63 s [1]; 1000 ÷ 63 = 15.9 [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. A drop of the mixture was added to iodine solution every 30 seconds, and the time until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 879, 399, 89, 107, 325; trial 2: 953, 404, 86, 109, 351; trial 3: 874, 397, 90, 111, 480. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Estimate the optimum temperature of the amylase from these results.
items.answer: (a) Volume and concentration of amylase; volume and concentration of starch. (b) About 40 °C (shortest time).
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: volume and concentration of amylase; volume and concentration of starch; pH (buffer); interval between samples; volume of iodine [2] (b) temperature with shortest time [1]; need more readings around it to be precise [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. (a) Calculate the rate of reaction at the optimum temperature, using rate = 1000 ÷ time. (b) Estimate the optimum temperature of the amylase from these results.
items.answer: (a) 14.4 s⁻¹ (arbitrary units) (b) About 40 °C (shortest time).
items.markingKey: (a) shortest mean time = 69.7 s [1]; 1000 ÷ 69.7 = 14.4 [1] [2] (b) temperature with shortest time [1]; need more readings around it to be precise [1] [2]

items.stem: Kenji mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. A drop of the mixture was added to iodine solution every 30 seconds, and the time until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: time for starch to disappear. (b) 82 s (c) Test more often than every 30 s to time the end-point more precisely.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = time for starch to disappear [1] [2] (b) (81 + 83 + 82) ÷ 3 [1] = 82 s [1] [2] (c) Any one from: test more often than every 30 s to time the end-point more precisely; leave the enzyme and starch at the temperature for 5 minutes before mixing (equilibrate); use a thermostatically controlled water bath; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: What is the optimum temperature of most human enzymes?
items.answer: About 37 °C
items.markingKey: Human enzymes work fastest at about body temperature.

items.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction fall at temperatures above the optimum?
options: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
The enzyme is digested by other enzymes
items.answer: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
items.markingKey: Denaturation: bonds in the protein break and the active site changes shape.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the effect of a low temperature and a high temperature on an enzyme.
items.answer: Low temperature: fewer collisions, slow rate, but enzyme not damaged and activity returns on warming. High temperature: enzyme denatured, active site permanently changed, activity lost.
items.markingKey: low = slow but reversible [1]; high = denatured, permanent [1] [2]

items.stem: A person has a fever of 41 °C. Suggest why a very high fever can be dangerous.
items.answer: Enzymes in the body start to denature above the optimum, so metabolic reactions slow down.
items.markingKey: enzymes denature [1]; reactions slow [1] [2]

items.stem: The time taken for an enzyme reaction to finish was measured at four temperatures: 25 °C: 75 s, 35 °C: 41 s, 45 °C: 76 s, 55 °C: 228 s. Calculate the rate (1000 ÷ time) at each temperature and state the temperature at which the enzyme was most active.

Kwame mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures. A drop of the mixture was added to iodine solution every 30 seconds, and the time until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 816, 379, 78, 126, 364; trial 2: 856, 368, 104, 126, 377; trial 3: 873, 366, 75, 121, 386. Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: The time for starch to disappear decreases as the temperature rises to 35 °C, which gives the lowest value, then increases. (A shorter time means a faster rate.)
items.markingKey: correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: The time taken for an enzyme reaction to finish was measured at four temperatures: 10 °C: 191 s, 25 °C: 75 s, 40 °C: 45 s, 55 °C: 228 s. Calculate the rate (1000 ÷ time) at each temperature and state the temperature at which the enzyme was most active.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a solution that keeps the pH constant at a chosen value"?
items.answer: Buffer solution
items.markingKey: Buffer solution: a solution that keeps the pH constant at a chosen value.

items.stem: Explain why amylase from saliva stops working when it reaches the stomach.
items.answer: The stomach has a low pH (acid); this is far from the optimum of amylase (about pH 7), so the active site changes shape and amylase is denatured.
items.markingKey: stomach acidic [1]; active site shape changed / denatured [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why different enzymes in the digestive system have different optimum pH values.
items.answer: Each enzyme works in a region with a particular pH (stomach acid, small intestine slightly alkaline); each has an active site shape that is most stable at that pH.
items.markingKey: different pH in regions [1]; active site best at that pH [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame added discs of potato (containing catalase) to hydrogen peroxide solution buffered at different pH values and measured the volume of oxygen collected in 2 minutes. Results table. pH: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. Volume of oxygen / cm³, trial 1: 1.5, 4.5, 27.3, 23.2, 2.6; trial 2: 1.6, 4.3, 29.1, 22.2, 2.5; trial 3: 1.5, 4.3, 28.3, 23.3, 2.7. items.answer: 14.12 cm³/min
items.markingKey: greatest mean = 28.23 cm³ [1]; ÷ 2 = 14.12 cm³/min [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how you could use a pH meter or universal indicator paper to check that a buffer is working during an enzyme experiment.
items.answer: Measure the pH of each mixture at the start and end; if the buffer is working, the pH stays the same.
items.markingKey: measure before and after [1]; pH unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the volume of oxygen collected from catalase and hydrogen peroxide can be used to measure the rate of reaction.
items.answer: Oxygen is a product; the more oxygen produced per minute, the faster the substrate is being broken down.
items.markingKey: oxygen is a product [1]; volume per unit time = rate [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Karachi states: "Acid kills enzymes in the stomach." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Enzymes are not alive; an unsuitable pH denatures them by changing the shape of the active site.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Enzymes are not alive; an unsuitable pH denatures them by changing the shape of the active site. [2]

items.answer: (a) salivary amylase: about pH 7; trypsin (a protease): about pH 8 (b) It would work slowly or not at all because the active site changes shape (denatured) away from its optimum pH.

items.stem: Describe and explain the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
items.answer: Rate increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, forming more ES complexes. Above the optimum the enzyme denatures: bonds break and the active site changes shape, so substrate no longer fits; rate falls to zero.
